title: Story of the Three Sharpers
summary: Three notorious tricksters met outside the city gates of Damascus: Haydar the Pickpocket, Mansur the Counterfeiter, and Qasim the Conjuro...
full_text:
Three notorious tricksters met outside the city gates of Damascus: Haydar the Pickpocket, Mansur the Counterfeiter, and Qasim the Conjuror.
'Brothers,' boasted Haydar, 'let each of us perform his masterpiece today; whoever pulls off the most audacious trick without using weapons shall be declared Master of the Guild.'

First went Haydar. He watched a wealthy farmer walking into the market leading a fat, prize ram by a hemp halter, with a little brass bell tied to the ram's tail so the farmer could hear it following.
Haydar sneaked behind, gently untied the bell from the ram, attached it to the farmer's belt loop, and led the prize ram away. The farmer walked half a mile, hearing the bell clinking behind him, until a neighbor laughed: 'Uncle, why art thou leading thine own coat tail?'

Next went Mansur. Finding the farmer weeping beside an open well, Mansur sat on the stone coping, crying loudly.
'Why weepest thou, friend?' asked the farmer.
'Woe is me!' sobbed Mansur. 'I dropped a casket containing two hundred gold dinars into this deep well. If an expert swimmer would dive and fetch it, I would gladly reward him with fifty dinars!'
The farmer thought: 'Here is my chance to recover my loss!' He stripped off his fine silk robes and boots, dove into the cold well water, and searched the muddy bottom for an hour. Meanwhile, Mansur scooped up the farmer's expensive clothes and boots and vanished!

Finally went Qasim. He observed the chief of police riding out with his patrol to apprehend the two tricksters. Qasim bought a pot of honey, covered himself in white sheepskins, climbed an ancient tombstone in the cemetery, and howled: 'I am the Guardian Spirit of the Tomb!'
When the captain approached, Qasim threw flour into his eyes, declared that whoever touched him would be transformed into a marble column, and took the captain's jeweled saddle while the patrol scattered in superstitious panic.

The three sharpers met at an inn to celebrate their spoils. But while they argued over whose trick was greatest, the clever baker's apprentice who overheard them locked their tavern door from the outside and alerted the municipal guard!

All three were marched before the governor. Their loot was returned to the poor farmer and the captain, while the three tricksters were sentenced to sweeping the public bazaar for three years, proving that those who spin webs of deceit eventually entangle their own feet.
moral: Trickery may succeed against the gullible for a day, but cleverness devoid of virtue ends in disgrace.
